paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making when the available collection of experts is too large to search directly. This situation arises in contextual and reinforcement learning, where experts can represent candidate policies. The aim is to compete with a powerful reference class without needing to enumerate every policy it contains.

The authors approach this through boosting: building a stronger learner from a weaker learning mechanism. They define the weaker mechanism through a multiplicative approximation guarantee on regret, which measures accumulated loss relative to a comparator. Given this access, their efficient algorithm achieves near-optimal regret against the convex hull of the base experts, meaning combinations of those experts.

The results cover both full feedback and partial, bandit feedback, where the learner receives more restricted information about its decisions. An analogous algorithm handles independently sampled statistical data. Together, these guarantees extend online and gradient boosting ideas across several learning settings, with the weak learner’s stated guarantee providing the foundation for the stronger result.
icml-2021-boosting-for-online-convex-opt.tldr: An efficient boosting method turns weak regret guarantees into near-optimal guarantees over combinations of experts, including under bandit feedback.

paragraphs: Distributed matrix multiplication divides work across machines, but slow workers can delay the overall computation. These workers, called stragglers, may still perform useful work even when they cannot finish as quickly as others. The paper considers a setup where a coordinating master assigns multiple tasks to each worker so that this computing capacity can contribute.

The proposed Chebyshev polynomial codes use a mechanism called task entanglement. Encoded matrices for different tasks are intertwined, reducing how many encoded matrices must be prepared for the multiple tasks assigned to a worker. This connects the organization of worker tasks directly to the cost of preparing and communicating their inputs.

The authors establish improvements in the scaling of encoding complexity at the master and communication load. Cloud experiments also demonstrate significant reductions in total matrix-multiplication processing time. The stated benefit therefore goes beyond recovering useful work from slow machines: the coding scheme reduces supporting costs that can otherwise offset the advantages of distributing the computation.
icml-2021-chebyshev-polynomial-codes-tas.tldr: Chebyshev polynomial codes intertwine distributed matrix-multiplication tasks to reduce encoding, communication, and observed processing costs.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning uncertain fields, such as electric fields or fluid flows. Here, an outcome is a field spread across space rather than a single value. Rotations and reflections matter because changing the spatial frame also changes how observations and predictions should be expressed.

The authors show that spatial invariance of a stochastic field requires an equivariant inference model. In plain terms, transforming the observations should transform the inferred field in the corresponding way. They investigate this requirement for two model families: fully characterizing equivariant Gaussian processes and introducing Steerable Conditional Neural Processes, or SteerCNPs, as a fully equivariant neural-process model.

Experiments cover Gaussian-process vector fields, images, and real weather data. The authors report significant improvements over previous models and better transfer-learning performance from equivariance. These findings connect the theoretical symmetry requirement to practical learning benefits in the evaluated settings: the model’s treatment of transformed data is built into its structure rather than left entirely to learning.
icml-2021-equivariant-learning-of-stocha.tldr: The paper characterizes equivariant Gaussian processes and introduces symmetry-preserving neural processes that improve field prediction and transfer in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper addresses federated user verification under two explicit constraints: each user has examples from only one class, and user embeddings cannot be shared with either the server or other users. Embeddings are the model’s vector representations of examples. The challenge is to learn a verification model collaboratively while keeping those representations unshared.

Federated User Verification, or FedUV, has users jointly learn a collection of vectors. Each user trains their instance embeddings to correlate strongly with a secret linear combination of those shared vectors. The authors show that selecting these combinations from error-correcting codewords enables collaborative training without revealing the users’ embedding vectors.

Experiments evaluate verification using voice, face, and handwriting data. FedUV performs on par with existing approaches while maintaining the stated restriction on embedding sharing. The contribution is a way to organize the training objective around shared structure and private combinations, showing that competitive verification performance is possible in the evaluated setting despite each user’s restricted local data.
icml-2021-federated-learning-of-user-ver.tldr: FedUV uses secret combinations of jointly learned vectors to train competitive federated verification models without sharing user embeddings.

paragraphs: Selecting useful features becomes difficult when information is distributed through nonlinear relationships and redundancies. A feature’s relevance can depend on how it interacts with other features and the label. This paper develops a Fourier-based way to analyze those relationships in supervised learning, with feature subset selection as a central application.

The authors first construct a Fourier expansion for functions of correlated binary random variables. This extends standard Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube beyond probability spaces where variables are independent. They also extend the analysis to stochastic mappings. These tools allow the feature-selection problem to be expressed through Fourier coefficients, which they connect to Bayesian classification error.

From this formulation, the authors derive a computationally efficient measure for choosing features. Their theoretical analysis establishes asymptotic optimality of the subsets selected using that measure, rather than a claim of optimality at every sample size. They also introduce an algorithm and report numerical experiments across several datasets, supporting the analysis as a practical approach to nonlinear feature-label dependence.
icml-2021-finding-relevant-information-v.tldr: A Fourier analysis for correlated binary variables yields an efficient feature-selection measure with an asymptotic optimality guarantee.

paragraphs: Episodic reinforcement-learning methods store past experience so an agent can quickly reuse successful behavior. The paper focuses on the difficulty of doing this in continuous domains, where exact states do not recur. Earlier episodic approaches also struggle to combine useful experience across different trajectories, limiting how effectively stored successes inform new decisions.

Generalizable Episodic Memory, or GEM, organizes remembered state-action values so they can generalize and support implicit planning over stored trajectories. Its memory therefore serves as more than a collection of isolated past outcomes. GEM also uses two estimators to reduce overestimation bias introduced when values propagate through the planning process.

On several MuJoCo continuous-control tasks, GEM significantly outperforms existing trajectory-based methods. Additional Atari experiments show significant improvements over baseline algorithms in a discrete-action setting. These results support both the continuous-domain motivation and broader applicability: organizing memory for generalization and controlling planning-related overestimation can make remembered experience more useful in the evaluated reinforcement-learning tasks.
icml-2021-generalizable-episodic-memory-.tldr: GEM makes episodic value memory generalizable and supports implicit planning, improving results on continuous-control tasks and Atari.

paragraphs: A generative model can assign higher likelihood to unfamiliar data than to data resembling its training set. This appears troubling if likelihood is treated as a direct measure of familiarity. The paper examines this behavior in hierarchical variational autoencoders, whose representations contain features at multiple levels.

The authors provide evidence that unfamiliar examples can nevertheless have familiar low-level features. Those features help explain why the model assigns high likelihood even when the example is outside the training distribution overall. They argue that recognizing such shared structure is expected and desirable, so the observed behavior need not mean that the density estimate itself is poor.

Using this explanation, the authors develop an unsupervised likelihood-ratio score for detecting out-of-distribution inputs. The score requires consistency with the training distribution across all feature levels rather than relying on overall likelihood alone. They describe the method as fast and scalable and report state-of-the-art detection results across many data and model combinations. The finding distinguishes modeling shared features from deciding whether an entire input is familiar.
icml-2021-hierarchical-vaes-know-what-th.tldr: Familiar low-level features explain some high likelihoods on unfamiliar inputs, motivating a multilevel likelihood-ratio detector.

paragraphs: Explaining a molecular graph neural network means identifying which parts of a molecule influenced its prediction. The paper asks whether changing how the network is trained can make those explanations more accurate and useful. It proposes two regularizers that shape the representations and prediction weights learned by graph convolutional neural networks.

Batch Representation Orthonormalization, or BRO, encourages node embeddings to be orthonormal: their directions are mutually perpendicular and their lengths normalized. Its motivation comes from molecular orbital theory. Gini regularization instead acts on the output-layer weights, restricting how many representation dimensions the model uses to predict. The two methods therefore constrain different stages of the model.

On artificial benchmarks, the regularizers can improve the accuracy of existing state-of-the-art attribution methods. In a real-world evaluation, medicinal chemists significantly prefer explanations from regularized models. These findings concern explanation quality and user preference, rather than a stated improvement in prediction accuracy. The authors study graph convolutional networks, while noting that both regularizers can also be applied to other neural networks.
icml-2021-improving-molecular-graph-neur.tldr: Two training regularizers improve molecular-network attribution quality on artificial benchmarks and produce explanations preferred by medicinal chemists.

paragraphs: Program synthesis must search a large space of possible programs to find one matching a specification. The paper takes inspiration from programmers who choose an overall structure before working out details. It proposes organizing synthesis into two levels: first predict a high-level plan, then generate a program guided by that plan.

The plans are learned representations expressed as sequences of discrete symbols. Discrete autoencoders provide a way to learn these latent codes from programs. Latent Programmer first predicts a code from input/output examples and then generates the program in the target language. This gives the search an intermediate representation between observed examples and complete program text.

The authors evaluate the method in two domains and report improved accuracy, particularly for longer programs, where search is especially difficult. The results support using learned plans to organize program generation. The central contribution is the two-level search structure: a compact representation captures a program’s broad organization before the synthesizer commits to the details of its implementation.
icml-2021-latent-programmer-discrete-lat.tldr: Latent Programmer predicts a discrete program plan before generating code, improving synthesis accuracy especially for longer programs.

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how a classifier’s test error changes as the number of training examples grows. The paper investigates how these curves can help evaluate choices in deep learning, including pretraining, architecture, and data augmentation. This makes performance across training-set sizes the object of analysis, extending earlier uses for parameter selection and performance extrapolation.

The authors propose a method for estimating learning curves robustly. They summarize the curve parameters through two concepts: error and data-reliance. These summaries are intended to make fitted curves useful for assessing model design choices, connecting prediction performance with its dependence on the amount of training data. They also evaluate different ways of parameterizing the curves.

Experiments illustrate how this approach can be used to analyze deep networks. The stated contribution is an analysis method and demonstrations of its use; the abstract does not identify a particular architecture or training technique as the winner. Its practical value is a structured way to examine how design decisions relate to both error and data requirements.
icml-2021-learning-curves-for-analysis-o.tldr: The paper develops robust learning-curve estimates to analyze how deep-network design choices affect error and reliance on training data.

paragraphs: A more accurate machine predictor does not automatically establish that the human using it will make better decisions. This paper makes human performance the direct target of learning. The machine’s role is to change how a problem is represented to a person, with the person still responsible for making the decision.

The proposed Mind Composed with Machine framework adapts representation learning to this human-facing purpose. It incorporates a model of human decision-making into the representation-learning process and uses a new human-in-the-loop training procedure. The representation is therefore optimized in connection with how people make decisions, rather than assessed solely by the accuracy of a machine predictor.

The authors empirically demonstrate successful applications across multiple tasks and forms of representation. These results support learning how to present a problem as a route to better human decision support. The broader contribution is to frame the machine and human as a combined decision-making process, so that the learning objective addresses the performance of the person the system is meant to help.
icml-2021-learning-representations-by-hu.tldr: Mind Composed with Machine learns problem representations optimized for human decision-making through a human-in-the-loop procedure.

paragraphs: Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning instead of consistently acting optimally. Existing analyses of reinforcement learning with linear function approximation had emphasized bounds growing like the square root of the number of interactions. This paper shows that much slower, logarithmic-type growth is attainable under two specified models of linear structure.

The crucial condition is a positive minimum suboptimality gap in the optimal action-value function. Suboptimal actions must be separated from optimal ones by a nonzero value difference. Under the linear MDP assumption, the authors establish a bound for LSVI-UCB involving log(T); under the linear mixture MDP assumption, they establish a bound for UCRL-VTR involving log cubed(T). Both also depend on feature dimension, episode length, and the inverse minimum gap.

The authors additionally prove gap-dependent lower bounds for both model classes. These provide complementary limits on achievable performance. The main message is conditional: linear structure together with a positive action-value gap permits stronger regret guarantees than the previously emphasized square-root dependence, with explicit costs for problem dimension, horizon, and action separation.
icml-2021-logarithmic-regret-for-reinfor.tldr: Under two linear MDP assumptions and a positive action-value gap, existing RL algorithms admit logarithmic-type regret bounds.

paragraphs: An LSTM is designed to retain information over time, but many systems also obey conservation laws governing how quantities can move or be redistributed. The paper introduces Mass-Conserving LSTM, or MC-LSTM, which incorporates this structure into the network. Its stored quantities are governed by conservation rather than treated only as unrestricted memory.

This architectural choice supplies an inductive bias suited to processes involving conserved amounts. The model extends the LSTM’s existing preference for retaining information to represent redistribution of those amounts. The authors demonstrate state-of-the-art results among neural arithmetic units on learning arithmetic operations, including addition tasks with a strong conservation structure.

The paper also applies MC-LSTM to traffic forecasting, pendulum modeling, and a large hydrology benchmark. It reports state-of-the-art peak-flow prediction on the hydrology task. In that application, internal states correlate with real-world processes, supporting their interpretability. Together, these findings show how encoding a conservation law can support both predictive performance and meaningful internal representations in the evaluated settings.
icml-2021-mc-lstm-mass-conserving-lstm-b.tldr: MC-LSTM builds conservation into recurrent memory, achieving strong arithmetic and hydrology results with interpretable states in the hydrology application.

paragraphs: Muesli is a reinforcement-learning policy update that combines regularized policy optimization with model learning as an auxiliary objective. The policy determines the agent’s actions, while learning a model supplies an additional training signal. The paper studies this combination as a way to improve policy optimization and achieve strong game-playing performance.

The reported Atari result is that Muesli matches MuZero’s state-of-the-art performance. Muesli selects actions directly with a policy network and does not use deep search. Its computation speed is comparable to model-free baselines. Together, these statements describe a useful empirical combination: high Atari performance alongside direct policy execution and the reported computational profile.

The Atari evaluation is accompanied by extensive ablations, which examine the contributions of components, and additional results on continuous control and 9x9 Go. The abstract’s explicit performance-matching claim concerns Atari. The broader contribution is a policy update that combines model learning with regularized optimization, demonstrating that these ingredients can work together effectively even when actions are produced without deep search.
icml-2021-muesli-combining-improvements-.tldr: Muesli combines regularized policy optimization and auxiliary model learning to match MuZero on Atari without deep search.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how randomness in optimization shapes the behavior of learned parameters. It models optimizer updates as discrete random recurrence relations and focuses on multiplicative noise, which can arise when local convergence rates vary. This differs from treating randomness only as an added disturbance of otherwise fixed update dynamics.

The authors show that multiplicative noise produces heavy-tailed stationary parameter behavior across a large class of models and optimizers. Heavy tails assign more probability to extreme values than light-tailed descriptions do. Their theory includes nonlinear and nonconvex models, along with momentum, Adam, and stochastic Newton methods. They also characterize dependence on step size, batch size, and data variability.

Those dependencies qualitatively resemble previously observed neural-network behavior. Further experiments illustrate that multiplicative noise and heavy-tailed structure improve movement between basins and exploration of nonconvex loss surfaces compared with the considered additive, light-tailed dynamics. This offers a mechanism linking optimizer randomness to exploration, supported by broad theoretical results and specific empirical demonstrations rather than a universal claim about training success.
icml-2021-multiplicative-noise-and-heavy.tldr: Multiplicative optimizer noise can produce heavy-tailed parameter behavior, with experiments linking that structure to better exploration of nonconvex losses.

paragraphs: The paper studies how multiple decision-making tasks can benefit from learning a shared representation. Its first setting consists of M concurrent linear bandits, each with dimension d, sharing a k-dimensional linear representation. The assumed shared dimension is much smaller than both the original feature dimension and the number of tasks.

The proposed MTLR-OFUL algorithm exploits that structure to improve regret over solving every task independently. Ignoring logarithmic factors, its bound is M times the square root of dkT, plus d times the square root of kMT, compared with Md times the square root of T for independent learning. A matching-oriented lower-bound analysis establishes near-optimality when d is greater than M.

The authors extend the algorithm and analysis to multitask episodic reinforcement learning with linear value-function approximation, assuming low inherent Bellman error. The contribution is theoretical evidence that shared representation learning can improve exploration efficiency. Its guarantees explicitly depend on common low-dimensional structure, with an additional approximation condition for the reinforcement-learning extension.
icml-2021-near-optimal-representation-le.tldr: Learning a shared low-dimensional representation improves multitask linear-bandit regret, with near-optimality in one regime and an extension to linear RL.

paragraphs: Agents trained together can develop arbitrary conventions that work with their training partners but fail with people or independently trained agents. Off-belief learning addresses this coordination problem by controlling the assumptions an agent makes about other agents’ past behavior. The aim is to avoid fragile chains of inference while retaining purposeful future cooperation.

At each step, the agent uses a policy optimized as though past actions came from a fixed reference policy, while future actions will follow the optimized policy itself. When the reference policy is uniformly random, the method converges to an optimal grounded policy that does not depend on behavioral inferences. Repeating the construction in a hierarchy introduces deeper reasoning in controlled stages.

The authors state that OBL converges to a unique policy, supporting coordination between agents that have not trained together. A fictitious-transition mechanism scales the approach to high-dimensional settings. Experiments show strong performance in a toy setting and Hanabi, a benchmark involving human–AI and zero-shot coordination. The approach makes assumptions about partners an explicit part of learning.
icml-2021-off-belief-learning-3af9e65fb1.tldr: Off-belief learning controls assumptions about past actions to learn uniquely determined policies suited to coordination with unfamiliar partners.

paragraphs: The paper studies the randomness of the Conjugate Kernel and Neural Tangent Kernel in ReLU networks at initialization. It derives exact distributions and moments for their diagonal entries. The focus is on how these quantities behave as network size changes, distinguishing ordinary feedforward networks from residual architectures.

For feedforward networks, when depth and width both tend to infinity, the diagonal values converge in distribution to log-normal variables. The variance of their logarithms scales with the depth-to-width ratio. For residual networks with infinitely many branches but fixed width, Conjugate Kernel diagonals instead approach a log-normal distribution whose log variance scales inversely with width.

The residual network’s Neural Tangent Kernel diagonals have a different limit: a log-normal variable multiplied by the Conjugate Kernel of a feedforward network. The authors interpret these results as suggesting that residual networks remain trainable with infinitely many branches and fixed width. Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis. The trainability statement is presented as an implication suggested by the kernel results, rather than a blanket guarantee for every training problem.
icml-2021-on-the-random-conjugate-kernel.tldr: Kernel-distribution results distinguish feedforward and residual scaling and suggest residual networks can remain trainable at fixed width with infinitely many branches.

paragraphs: The paper considers classification objectives available only as black-box functions of the confusion matrix, which summarizes correct and incorrect predictions by class. Such objectives arise when a learner can query a metric but cannot directly optimize its formula, or when performance must be estimated from a small validation sample under label noise or domain change.

The method adaptively learns weights for training examples so that a weighted training objective approximates the desired validation metric. The authors describe how to model and estimate these weights. They then use them to iteratively adjust a pretrained class-probability estimator, turning its probability estimates into a classifier aligned with the target metric.

The paper analyzes the procedure’s statistical properties and evaluates it in settings involving noisy labels, domain shifts, and fair classification. Results compare favorably with state-of-the-art baselines for the respective applications. The central idea is to use validation feedback to reshape example importance, creating a usable training objective for a performance measure that is not directly accessible to ordinary optimization.
icml-2021-optimizing-black-box-metrics-w.tldr: Adaptive example weights translate black-box validation metrics into objectives used to iteratively adjust a pretrained classifier.

paragraphs: PipeTransformer addresses the computing and engineering costs of training large Transformer models across multiple devices. Its central idea is to adapt the distributed training arrangement as some layers become frozen. This links decisions about which layers continue learning to decisions about how hardware is allocated during the remaining training.

An adaptive algorithm gradually identifies and freezes layers while training is running. The system removes those layers from the training pipeline and packs the active layers onto fewer GPUs. It then creates more replicas to expand data-parallel processing. Freezing therefore triggers a reorganization of the computation, allowing available resources to support more parallel work on the layers still being trained.

The authors evaluate Vision Transformer on ImageNet and BERT on SQuAD and GLUE. They report speedups of up to 2.83 times relative to a state-of-the-art baseline without losing accuracy in those evaluations. Performance analyses examine the algorithm and system design, and the implementation provides modular APIs. The results demonstrate the benefit of coordinating layer freezing with flexible distributed execution.
icml-2021-pipetransformer-automated-elas.tldr: PipeTransformer freezes layers and reallocates GPUs during training, reporting up to 2.83-fold speedup without accuracy loss in its evaluations.

paragraphs: SoundDet detects and locates overlapping, moving sound events directly from multichannel audio waveforms. The paper treats each event as a complete object extending through time and space. This addresses the partial detections associated with segment-wise approaches and avoids first converting the waveform into a time-frequency representation for an image-processing pipeline.

The lightweight, end-to-end framework combines a shared backbone with separate temporal-detection and spatial-localization heads. Its learned filters preserve phase and frequency information needed to retain direction-of-arrival cues, while improving computational and parameter efficiency over standard convolutions. A dense proposal map provides candidate events across widely varying durations.

Two accompanying maps assess proposals through temporal overlap and motion smoothness. These connect confidence to both event timing and consistency of movement, unifying temporal and spatial training. Experiments on the public DCASE dataset show advantages under segment-based evaluation and the authors’ new event-based evaluation. The results support processing sounds as complete moving events rather than assessing their temporal and spatial structure in isolation.
icml-2021-sounddet-polyphonic-moving-sou.tldr: SoundDet jointly detects and localizes complete moving sound events from raw multichannel audio, showing advantages on DCASE evaluations.

paragraphs: A backdoor attack corrupts a small part of a training set so that the trained model behaves differently when an attacker’s watermark appears. The model can remain accurate on ordinary inputs, allowing the compromise to go unnoticed. This paper addresses detecting poisoned examples when their small number makes their signal difficult to distinguish.

Earlier defenses examine intermediate model representations to separate poisoned and clean data. Their effectiveness can depend on having enough corrupted examples to create a visible spectral signature, a pattern in the representations’ variation. SPECTRE uses robust covariance estimation to amplify that signature, making the structure associated with corruption easier to detect.

The authors report that the defense completely removes backdoors whenever the evaluated benchmark attacks succeed, including regimes where previous methods cannot detect the poisoned examples. That claim is tied to the benchmark attacks rather than all possible attacks. The contribution is a statistical method for strengthening a weak corruption signal, addressing the difficulty of finding a small poisoned subset within mostly clean training data.
icml-2021-spectre-defending-against-back.tldr: SPECTRE amplifies poisoned-data signatures with robust covariance estimation and removes successful backdoors across the evaluated benchmark attacks.

paragraphs: Min-max optimization involves competing directions of improvement and can produce cycles instead of settling at a solution. Although these behaviors are well understood in convex-concave problems, many machine-learning applications fall outside that setting. This paper analyzes what popular optimization methods can converge to in nonconvex, nonconcave problems.

The authors show that a broad class of algorithms and heuristics may approach spurious attractors with arbitrarily high probability. These are sets that draw in the algorithm’s behavior despite containing neither min-max solutions nor stationary points. Consequently, apparent convergence to a stable pattern of behavior can occur without reaching even a point where the relevant gradients vanish.

The paper demonstrates these attractors in simple two-dimensional examples, corroborating the theoretical claims. The result identifies a possible failure mode of many methods and a pitfall for theoretical frameworks that overlook such limiting behavior. It does not say every run must fail; it establishes that high-probability convergence itself can be misleading when the object attracting the algorithm is unrelated to the desired optimality conditions.
icml-2021-the-limits-of-min-max-optimiza.tldr: Many min-max algorithms can converge with arbitrarily high probability to attractors containing neither optimal nor stationary points.

paragraphs: Many prediction records are naturally sets: they contain a variable number of items whose order is arbitrary. A patient’s prescribed medications provide one example. Ordinary fixed-size representations do not directly match this structure. Set-Tree extends tree-based models so they can work with such collections as sets.

The method introduces attention and split criteria compatible with set inputs. These changes bring support for sets to model families such as random forests and gradient boosting. The paper also examines theoretical properties and explains how Set-Trees support item-level explanations, connecting a prediction to individual members of the input collection.

Experiments span problems including subatomic particle jets and galaxy redshift estimation. Across the evaluated problems, Set-Tree consistently and significantly outperforms existing tree-based approaches. It is also competitive with deep learning and often exceeds its performance. The findings establish set-aware trees as a strong option in these evaluations, combining the ability to process variable-size collections with explanations that can refer to particular items.
icml-2021-trees-with-attention-for-set-p.tldr: Set-Tree adds attention and set-compatible splits to tree models, delivering strong empirical performance and item-level explainability.

paragraphs: The paper studies online optimization with particularly limited feedback. At each stage, the learner faces an unknown nonconvex loss function and observes only the loss incurred by its own choice. It therefore must learn how to act without receiving gradients or a full description of the current loss landscape.

The proposed hierarchical dual-averaging approach builds an online model that accumulates loss information over time. It has two main components: a regularizer adapted to the Fisher information metric and an exploration schedule organized hierarchically across the state space. The regularizer uses an information-based geometry, while the schedule structures how the learner explores possible choices.

Together, these components enable sharper control of the model’s bias and variance. The authors use that control to derive tight bounds for both static and dynamic regret, covering comparison with a fixed hindsight choice and with a changing hindsight policy. The contribution links limited-feedback exploration and model geometry to theoretical guarantees in a setting where nonconvex losses and unavailable gradients make learning difficult.
icml-2021-zeroth-order-non-convex-learni.tldr: Hierarchical dual averaging combines information-based regularization and structured exploration to obtain tight regret bounds from loss-only feedback.
